{{short description|Probability theorem}}
{{dablink|Not to be confused with: the [[Ionescu-Tulcea–Marinescu ergodic theorem]].}}

In the mathematical [[theory of probability]], the '''Ionescu-Tulcea theorem''', sometimes called the '''Ionesco Tulcea extension theorem''', deals with the existence of [[probability measure]]s for probabilistic events consisting of a countably infinite number of individual probabilistic events. In particular, the individual events may be [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]] or dependent with respect to each other. Thus, the statement goes beyond the mere existence of countable [[product measure]]s. The theorem was proved by [[Cassius Ionescu-Tulcea]] in 1949.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Ionescu Tulcea, C. T.|title=Mesures dans les espaces produits|journal=Atti Accad. Naz. Lincei Rend.|volume=7|year=1949|pages=208–211}}</ref><ref name=Shalizi>{{cite web|author=Shalizi, Cosma|author-link=Cosma Shalizi|website=Cosma Shalizi, CMU Statistics, Carnegie Mellon University|title=Chapter 3. Building Infinite Processes from Regular Conditional Probability Distributions|url=https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/754/notes/lecture-03.pdf}} [https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/754/notes/ Index of /~cshalizi/754/notes] {{cite web|website=stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi|title=''Almost None of the Theory of Stochastic Processes: A Course on Random Processes, for Students of Measure-Theoretic Probability, with a View to Applications in Dynamics and Statistics'' by Cosma Rohilla Shalizi with Aryeh Kontorovich|url=http://stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/almost-none/}}</ref>

==Statement of the theorem==
Suppose that <math> (\Omega_0, \mathcal A_0, P_0) </math> is a [[probability space]] and <math> (\Omega_i, \mathcal A_i) </math> for <math> i \in \N </math> is a sequence of [[measurable space]]s. For each <math> i \in \N </math> let
:<math> \kappa_i \colon (\Omega^{i-1}, \mathcal A^{i-1}) \to (\Omega_i, \mathcal A_i) </math>
be the [[Markov kernel]] derived from <math> (\Omega^{i-1}, \mathcal A^{i-1}) </math> and <math> (\Omega_i, \mathcal A_i), </math>, where

:<math> \Omega^i:=\prod_{k=0}^i\Omega_k \text{ and } \mathcal A^i:= \bigotimes_{k=0}^i \mathcal A_k.</math>

Then there exists a sequence of probability measures
:<math> P_i:=P_0 \otimes \bigotimes_{k=1}^i \kappa_k </math> defined on the product space for the sequence <math> (\Omega^i, \mathcal A^i) </math>, <math> i \in \N, </math>
and there exists a uniquely defined probability measure <math> P </math> on <math> \left(\prod_{k=0}^\infty \Omega_k, \bigotimes_{k=0}^\infty \mathcal A_k\right) </math>, so that
:<math> P_i(A)=P\left( A \times \prod_{k=i+1}^\infty \Omega_k \right) </math>

is satisfied for each <math> A \in \mathcal A^i </math> and <math> i \in\N </math>. (The measure <math> P </math> has [[Conditional probability|conditional probabilities]] equal to the stochastic kernels.)<ref name=Abate>{{cite journal|author=Abate, Alessandro|author2=Redig, Frank|author3=Tkachev, Ilya|title=On the effect of perturbation of conditional probabilities in total variation|year=2014|journal=Statistics & Probability Letters|volume=88|pages=1–8|doi=10.1016/j.spl.2014.01.009|arxiv=1311.3066}} [https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.3066 arXiv preprint]</ref>

==Applications==
The construction used in the proof of the Ionescu-Tulcea theorem is often used in the theory of [[Markov decision process]]es, and, in particular, the theory of [[Markov chain]]s.<ref name=Abate/>
